unit.title: Develop and implement work unit plan

summary: This unit teaches you to plan the yearly work of a unit in a public body: link the plan to the corporate plan, consult the team and customers, write SMART objectives and performance measures, schedule activities with owners and milestones, work out capacity and budget, plan for risks, get the plan approved, put it into action, monitor progress, adjust it and evaluate it at the end of the year. It is written for section heads, unit managers and supervisors in Jamaican ministries, agencies and municipal corporations.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. Every unit in a public body (a records section, a customer service unit, a licensing office, an outreach team) is expected to know what it is there to achieve, what it will do this year, who will do it, with what money and people, and how it will know if it worked. The document that answers those questions is the **work unit plan**.

A work unit plan is the unit's plan for a period, usually the **financial year**. In the Jamaican public sector the financial year runs from **1 April to 31 March**. The plan turns the organisation's strategy into the unit's actual work. The agency's **strategic or corporate plan** says where the whole organisation is going over several years; the unit plan says what this unit will do this year to help it get there.
**Who it is for:** section heads, unit managers and supervisors who must write, run and report on a unit plan, and trainees who want to show they can manage a unit's work.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Link the plan to the corporate plan
Start from the body's priorities and show how each unit objective supports them.
Involve staff, other units and the public in setting priorities and targets.
Write SMART objectives with indicators, baselines and targets; tell outputs from outcomes.
List activities with owners, dates, milestones and dependencies, and show them on a Gantt chart.
Work out staff hours (capacity) against workload, cost the plan and compare with the ceiling.
Name risks and assumptions, rate them and plan responses and contingencies.
Get approval and brief the team
Take the plan to the director, then brief staff and give each person an individual work plan.
Review progress regularly, report, correct, revise with approval and learn at year end.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** of scenario questions on plans, measures, scheduling, capacity, budgets, monitoring and reporting, including short sums.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms such as variance, RACI, deliverable, contingency plan) and longer answers in full sentences.
**Group practical tasks**: develop a work unit plan from a case pack, and run a quarterly progress review and revise the plan. Each member has a named role.

blocks.note: Work every sum twice, by two different routes. Targets, hours and budgets are used to judge you and your team for a year.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Starting from the corporate plan and consulting people

flow: National and sector priorities (such as the national development plan and the government's stated priorities)
The ministry's or agency's strategic and corporate plan
The division's or department's operational plan
The work unit plan for the year

blocks.p: A unit plan is built **on the priorities of the strategic and corporate plan first**. If a unit's work does not support a corporate priority, ask why the unit is doing it. A director who says the strategic plan and the unit plan 'do different jobs' is right: the strategic plan sets direction over several years, and a unit plan turns it into the unit's **yearly work**.

head: Source
What it tells you
rows: The priorities and targets the unit must support
What was achieved and missed, and why
How many applications, inspections or enquiries to expect
Who is available, skills, planned leave
How much money the unit can spend
What help is needed from or owed to finance, IT, human resources and others

blocks.p: Staff know the work best and are **more committed to a plan they helped to make**. Hold a planning meeting, ask for ideas, test targets with those who must deliver them, and use their answers. If some team members say the targets are too high, **listen to their reasons and review the evidence**; do not simply insist, and do not simply lower the targets without checking.
A unit that serves the public should read complaints, surveys and comments, because they show where service needs to improve. A plan that ignores them may repeat last year's problems.

If a project needs help from the finance and IT units, **agree the support and timing with them early**, while planning, not after the plan is approved. If your service cannot start until the IT unit sets up the system, that is a **dependency**, and the dependency must be in the plan.

blocks.note: In the Jamaican public sector, plans are submitted and approved through the ministry's planning and corporate services channels. Follow your body's template and deadlines, and keep the plan consistent with your approved budget.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Objectives, outputs, outcomes and performance measures

blocks.p: A work unit plan usually begins with the unit's **purpose** (why it exists) and its **objectives** (what it will achieve this year).
A **SMART objective** is specific, **measurable** (progress can be checked with figures or other clear evidence), achievable, relevant and time-bound.

head: Weak
SMART
rows: Scan all 2015-2020 property files by 30 June
Cut the average time from receipt to decision from 18 to 12 working days by 31 December
Hold 24 community outreach sessions in six districts by 31 March

blocks.p: Three to five objectives are enough for most units. Too many objectives scatter effort.

head: Term
Meaning
Example: public health education unit
rows: What goes in: money, staff, time
Run sessions in schools and churches
What the work produces; usually countable
Fewer cases of dengue in the target communities
A specific thing the unit must produce
A report, a database, a trained group of staff

blocks.p: An **output** is what you do; an **outcome** is what changes because of it. Measuring only outputs can hide failure: 40 sessions is not success if dengue cases have not fallen. Measure both where you can.
An **indicator** is the figure you track. Choose indicators that really show the objective and that you can collect cheaply.

head: Objective
Good indicator
Weak indicator
rows: Average working days from receipt to decision
Number of staff in the unit
Percentage of surveyed customers rating service good or better
Number of files awaiting action at month end

ul: **Baseline**: the starting figure (for example 18 days).
**Target**: where you want to be (12 days).
**Service standard**: a published promise to customers, such as 'all customer letters will be answered within 10 working days'.
**Efficiency**: making the best use of staff time and money to produce results. For example, cost per application = total cost / number processed: J$7,200,000 / 2,400 = J$3,000.

blocks.p: Spread yearly targets over the months if the work is steady: 4,800 applications a year is 4,800 / 12 = **400 a month**, 1,200 a quarter. 2,700 inspections a year is 225 a month. If the work has peaks (for example, renewals at year end), set monthly targets to match.

blocks.note: Every target needs a baseline and a way of collecting the data. Without them, you cannot tell if you are on course.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: For each objective, list the **activities** needed, who will lead each, when it starts and ends, and what it produces. Prioritise: if the unit has more requests than it can handle, **rank tasks by their link to objectives, urgency and impact**.

head: Tool or term
What it shows or means
rows: Activities as bars across a timeline, so overlaps and dates can be seen
A key date or point: for example, finishing all files in one building by 30 June
An activity that cannot start until another is finished or provided
Time needed before an event: invitations must go out six weeks before a training event

blocks.p: **Worked example:** activity A (6 weeks) starts on 3 May. Activity B (4 weeks) cannot start until A ends. A ends after 6 weeks, on 14 June; B then ends 4 weeks later, on **12 July**. A delay of two weeks in A pushes B's end to 26 July.
**Date counting:** a training event on 1 October needs invitations six weeks (42 days) before: 1 October minus 42 days is **20 August**. Work back carefully and check against a calendar.
Check the calendar for public holidays, school terms, the Christmas period, hurricane season (June to November) and the financial year end.
Every activity needs a **named person responsible**, so it is clear who leads it and answers for it. When allocating tasks, consider **skills, workload balance and development needs**.

head: RACI letter
Meaning
rows: The one person who answers for the final result
Gives advice before the work is done

blocks.p: Each activity should have **one** accountable person. The **unit manager is accountable** for making sure the work unit plan is delivered, with each officer accountable for their own tasks.

Each officer's **individual work plan** is drawn from the unit plan. It records the officer's tasks, targets and dates for the year and shows the officer's part in the unit plan. It links to the staff performance appraisal system, so that what officers are assessed on is what the unit has agreed to deliver.

blocks.note: A plan in which everyone is 'responsible' is a plan in which nobody is. Put one name against each activity.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **Capacity** is the productive time the unit's people have. Not every working hour is productive: allow for leave, public holidays, training, meetings and sickness. A typical planning figure might be about 1,500 to 1,700 productive hours a year per full-time officer; use the figure your body gives.

head: Step
Sum
Example
rows: Number of items x hours each, plus other fixed work
Prioritise, seek resources, or agree different targets

blocks.p: If the draft plan shows more work than staff can do, the manager should **prioritise, seek more resources or agree to change the targets**. Do not hide the gap and hope. Allow for known absences: if two of eight officers usually take long leave in July, schedule the work and cover around it.

Overtime is extra paid hours at a higher rate. 300 extra hours at J$1,500 an hour cost 300 x 1,500 = **J$450,000**. Compare with other ways of closing the gap (a temporary officer, shifting work, reducing a target) and consider fatigue and the effect on service.

Plan for all resources the work needs: **staff, vehicles, fuel, materials, equipment, accommodation, IT and budget**. A community outreach drive in four parishes needs more than officers: it needs transport, fuel, handouts and refreshments.

Cost each activity and add up: salaries are usually budgeted separately, but travel, training, printing, supplies and overtime come from the unit's budget. Stay within the **budget ceiling** the ministry sets for the unit.

head: Measure
Formula
Example
rows: Budget J$4,000,000, spent J$3,800,000: underspend J$200,000
Compare the share spent with the share of the year gone
Training budget J$1,200,000; J$900,000 (75%) spent by the half year: ahead of plan, so check

blocks.note: Variance is a signal, not a verdict. A variance may be good (an early saving) or bad (a cost out of control). Always find out why.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Plans meet surprises. A good plan names the main **risks to delivery**, rates them and says what will be done.

head: Risk
Likelihood
Impact
Response
rows: Back up files off site; contingency plan to work from another site; plan activity dates outside peak season where possible
Key officer leaves or is on long leave
Cross-train; plan cover; schedule around known leave
New system late from the IT unit
Agree dates with IT early; keep the old process until go-live
Prioritise activities so those that can be dropped are known
Personal data leaked from a survey

blocks.p: A **contingency plan** is a back-up plan to use if a key risk happens. Name who will act and what they will do.
State the **key assumptions** in the plan, such as 'the new software will be live by July'. If an assumption turns out to be wrong, the plan can be adjusted. Check assumptions at each review.

If the plan includes collecting personal information from residents (for example in a survey), include **steps to protect the data as the law requires**: collect only what is needed, store it securely, restrict access, and delete it when no longer needed. The data protection law exists to protect personal data and limit its use.
Some things do not belong in a work unit plan: an individual officer's medical history is private and has no place in it. The plan lists officers' roles and workloads, not private details.

blocks.note: After a hurricane or flood, the plan can be revised: tell those affected, agree changes with the director, and record what was dropped and why.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: After drafting, the section head should **get the plan approved by the director as the agency requires** before work on it begins. Approval confirms that the plan fits the corporate plan, the budget and the law, and gives the manager authority to proceed.

Once approved, **brief the team and link tasks to each person**. Explain the purpose, the objectives, the targets, the timetable, the roles and how progress will be checked. Give each officer a written individual work plan. Allow questions and note any concerns.

blocks.h: Getting started: the first three months

flow: Brief the whole unit and give out individual work plans
Confirm the support promised by other units (finance, IT, HR)
Set up simple records and a tracking sheet for each indicator
Book the monthly progress meetings for the year
Start the first priority activities and early milestones
Review after the first month and fix any early problems

ul: If a new officer is struggling with a task, **coach the officer and adjust timing if needed**.
Match tasks to skills, and give development opportunities.
When the unit meets its half-year targets, **recognise the team and share what worked**.
Listen to staff suggestions: if a team member proposes a simpler way to process requests, **test it and, if it works, update the procedure**.

blocks.p: Keep in contact with the other units on which your plan depends. A short regular meeting or message can prevent a month of delay.

blocks.note: Staff who are told what the plan is, why it matters, and what is expected of them each month are far more likely to deliver it than staff who first see it in a quarterly report.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: **Monitoring** means regularly checking progress against the plan. Review **regularly, such as monthly, with the team**, at a **progress meeting**. Keep it short and focused on the indicators, milestones and budget.
Collect data with **simple records kept as the work is done** (a daily tally, a register, a spreadsheet), not a big exercise at the end.

head: Check
Method
Example
rows: 1,050 returns processed against 1,200 in a quarter: 87.5%
File scanning in building 1 complete by 30 June?
Is the new software still due in July?

flow: Find out why: ask the team, check the records
Decide whether the cause is temporary (illness) or lasting (target too high)
Agree corrective action with a name and a date
Tell the director if the plan or budget may be affected
Follow up at the next meeting

blocks.p: If one activity is **two months behind**, first find out why and agree corrective action. Do not blame, and do not wait for the year end.
A monthly or quarterly report to the director should contain **progress against targets, issues and support needed**. Be honest: say what has been achieved and what has not.

A plan can be changed when circumstances change, for example a hurricane damages the office or the ministry directs the unit to take on a new national drive. **Revise the plan with approval and tell those affected.** Re-check capacity, budget and timing, decide what to drop or delay, and update the targets and the individual work plans.

At the end of the year, **review results and lessons to shape the next plan**: which objectives were met, what did the indicators show, what went wrong and why, what did customers say, what should be done differently? Share the results with the team.

head: Plan type
Purpose
Time
rows: All the unit's regular work and priorities for the year
One piece of work with a start, end and set result

blocks.p: When a unit runs a project alongside its normal work, include the project in the work unit plan as an activity with its own milestones, and count the project's staff hours in the capacity sums.

ul: explain how a work unit plan relates to the corporate plan, and name the Jamaican financial year.
involve the team, customers and other units in planning, and respond to team concerns.
write SMART objectives with baselines and targets, and tell outputs from outcomes.
choose indicators and set a service standard.
convert yearly targets to monthly ones.
list activities with owners, dates, milestones and dependencies, and draw a Gantt chart.
use a RACI chart and write an individual work plan.
work capacity, workload and gap, and deal with a shortfall.
cost a plan, and calculate cost per unit, variance and overspend percentage.
list risks, assumptions and contingencies, and protect personal data.
get the plan approved and brief the team.
monitor progress with simple records and report to the director.
correct delays and revise the plan with approval.
evaluate the plan at year end and use the lessons.

terms: The unit's plan for a period, usually the financial year.
The body's multi-year plan of its aims and priorities.
The government's budget year, in Jamaica 1 April to 31 March.
Specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.
Progress can be checked with figures or clear evidence.
A specific thing the unit must produce.
A published promise to customers, such as a time limit.
A chart of activities as bars across a timeline.
A key date or point in the plan.
An activity that cannot start until another is done or provided.
A chart of who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed.
The productive hours the unit's people have.
The difference between a planned figure and the actual result.
A back-up plan if a key risk happens.
An officer's own tasks and targets for the year, drawn from the unit plan.
A regular meeting, often monthly, to check progress against the plan.

c1.title: The public health inspection unit in St Mary
c1.text: The public health inspection unit of a municipal corporation in St Mary has 9 officers, each with about 1,500 productive hours a year. Next year it must carry out 2,400 inspections of food vendors, each taking about 3 hours, run a dengue and hygiene education campaign needing 4,800 hours, and spend 1,800 hours on administration. The unit head, Mr Winston Bailey, must write the plan within a budget ceiling that allows overtime at J$1,600 an hour.

c2.title: The unit budget at the half year
c2.text: A social services unit in Westmoreland has a budget of J$6,400,000 for the financial year, planned to be spent evenly. At the end of September, the end of the second quarter, the unit has spent J$3,520,000. Most of the overspend is on fuel for field visits and printing. The manager, Mrs Angela Thompson, is preparing her half-year report to the director.

c3.title: Scheduling an online appointment service
c3.text: A licensing unit plans to launch an online appointment service. Activity A, building the booking system by the IT unit, takes 6 weeks and starts on 3 May. Activity B, training the unit's 12 officers, takes 4 weeks and cannot start until A ends. Staff must be invited to a launch event on 12 March, and invitations must go out five weeks (35 days) before. The unit head, Mr Dwight Brown, must show these dates on the plan.

c4.title: A records unit in Clarendon at the first quarter
c4.text: A records unit in Clarendon has a yearly target of 2,000 files digitised, spread evenly. At the end of the first quarter, 410 files have been done. One activity, training staff on the new software, is two months behind because the IT unit has not delivered the system. Later in the year the ministry directs the unit to take on a national registration drive that was not in the plan. A newly hired officer is struggling with the scanning equipment.

c5.title: Patient records in a parish hospital
c5.text: A hospital's patient records unit has an average wait of 12 days for a copy of a record. The objective in the new plan is to cut it to 6 days by December. A survey of 150 patients found that 108 were satisfied with the service. Staff say the target is too ambitious, because records are in three buildings. The plan also says that all requests will be acknowledged within 2 working days.

questions.q: Each officer is given about 1,500 productive hours, not the full hours in a working year. Why?
o: Leave, holidays, training, meetings and sickness take time that cannot be used on the unit's work
Officers are expected to work only on the busiest tasks, so the remaining hours are not counted
Overtime hours are always deducted from the officer's normal hours in the plan
The ministry reduces each officer's hours to save money on the unit's budget
questions.why: Capacity is the time actually available for the unit's work. Planning on gross hours overstates capacity and leads to targets that cannot be met.

questions.q: What is the total workload, and what is the gap?
o: 13,800 hours, a shortfall of 300 hours
13,800 hours, a spare 300 hours
7,200 hours, a spare 6,300 hours
6,600 hours, a shortfall of 6,900 hours

questions.q: What would 300 hours of overtime cost at J$1,600 an hour?
What should Mr Bailey do about the gap in the draft plan?
o: Prioritise, seek resources such as overtime, or agree changed targets with the director
Leave the gap as it is and hope that fewer absences occur than in past years
Cut the officers' training time and use those hours for inspections instead
Lower the standard of the checks slightly so the same work takes fewer hours
questions.why: A plan that shows more work than staff can do must be fixed openly: prioritise, resource the gap or change targets, with agreement from the director.

questions.q: How much was the unit planned to have spent by the end of September, and what is the variance?
o: J$3,200,000 planned; J$320,000 overspent
J$3,520,000 planned; nothing overspent so far
J$3,200,000 planned; J$320,000 underspent
J$6,400,000 planned; J$2,880,000 underspent

questions.q: If spending continues at the same rate, what will the total overspend be for the year, as a percentage of the budget?
What is the most useful first step for Mrs Thompson?
o: Find out why fuel and printing are over, then agree corrective action
Stop all field visits at once until the new financial year begins
Leave the figures out of the report until the year-end review is due
Ask the director for extra money without explaining the overspend
questions.why: A variance is a signal. Find the cause, decide if it is temporary or lasting, and agree action before reporting.

questions.q: What should the half-year report to the director contain?
o: Progress against targets, the variance with reasons, issues and support needed
Only the targets that have been met, to keep the report positive
A full list of the leave days taken by each officer in the unit
A statement that spending will improve in the second half of the year
questions.why: A good report is honest and complete: results against targets, issues and what help is needed.

questions.q: When will Activity B, the training, end if A starts on 3 May and goes to plan?
o: 12 July
14 June
31 May
26 July
questions.why: A runs 6 weeks to 14 June; B runs 4 weeks after that, to 12 July. B cannot start before A ends.

questions.q: A is two weeks late. What happens to B?
o: It ends two weeks later, on 26 July, because it depends on A
It still ends on 12 July, since training can begin before the system is ready
It is cancelled and the officers are trained after the launch instead
It ends on 28 June, because delays are absorbed by the training period
questions.why: B depends on A, so any delay in A passes straight to B: 12 July + 14 days = 26 July.

questions.q: By what date must invitations to the 12 March event go out?
o: 5 February
12 February
26 February
19 January
questions.why: 35 days before 12 March: 12 March - 12 days = 28 February, then 23 more days back = 5 February (February has 28 days in a non-leap year).

questions.q: In the plan, what is the start of training dependent on?
o: A dependency: the training cannot start until the IT unit has finished the system
A milestone: the training is simply a date that the unit head has chosen
A deliverable: the training is a document produced by the licensing unit
An outcome: the training is the change that results for customers
questions.why: A dependency is an activity that cannot start until another is done or provided. The completion date of the system could be a milestone, but the link between the two is the dependency.

questions.q: What percentage of the first quarter's target of files has been completed?
What should the unit head do first about the training activity that is two months behind?
o: Find out why and agree corrective action and dates with the IT unit
Wait until the year end to see whether the delay corrects itself
Raise it in the next team meeting as a failure by the unit's own staff
Take the training out of the plan without informing the director
questions.why: The cause is the late system. Find out why, agree corrective action and dates with the unit responsible, and tell the director if the plan is affected.

questions.q: How should the manager deal with the new national registration drive?
o: Revise the plan with approval, re-check capacity and tell those affected
Accept the drive and keep every other target unchanged without comment
Refuse the drive, because it was not part of the approved plan
Add the work on top of normal duties and record nothing of the change
questions.why: Changes during the year need a revised plan with approval, checking capacity, budget and timing, and telling those affected about what moves.

questions.q: The registration drive will run as a three-month project alongside normal work. How should it appear in the unit plan?
o: As an activity with its own milestones, with its staff hours counted in capacity
As a separate plan kept outside the unit plan so that it does not affect targets
As a note at the end of the plan, with no hours or dates given
As a replacement for the normal work of the unit during those three months
questions.why: A project run alongside normal work belongs in the unit plan with its milestones, and its hours must be counted in the capacity sums so that other targets are adjusted honestly.

questions.q: Which is an outcome rather than an output for the records unit?
o: A shorter wait for patients to get a copy of their record
The number of records retrieved by the unit in a month
The number of staff trained on the new filing system
The number of boxes of files moved between the buildings
questions.why: An outcome is the change that results for customers. Counts of work done are outputs.

questions.q: What percentage of patients surveyed were satisfied, and how should this be used?
o: 72%, as a baseline for measuring change in the next survey
108%, as a target for the unit to reach next year
28%, since this is the number of patients who were satisfied
72%, a figure that can be ignored because it comes from a survey
questions.why: 108 / 150 = 0.72 = 72%. A baseline is the starting measurement that later results are compared with.

questions.q: Staff say the target of 6 days is too ambitious. What should the manager do?
o: Listen to their reasons, review the evidence, then confirm or revise the target
Tell them that targets are set by management and are not open to discussion
Lower the target to 12 days at once without looking at any evidence
Remove the waiting-time target from the plan altogether
questions.why: Involving staff improves plans. Review the evidence (for example, the three buildings) before confirming or changing a target.

questions.q: 'All requests will be acknowledged within 2 working days.' What is this an example of?
o: A service standard
A baseline
A deliverable
A dependency
questions.why: A service standard is a published promise to customers about the quality or speed of service.
